nodes.title: Okta Universal Directory & SSO: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Okta's Universal Directory is a centralized cloud store of all user profiles and attributes, aggregated from many sources. Combined with sign-on policies and SSO, it lets users authenticate once and reach many apps—a core Okta certification topic.

flashcards.front: What is profile sourcing (mastering) in Universal Directory?
flashcards.back: It designates an authoritative source—such as Active Directory, an HR system, or Okta itself—as the master for a user's profile. Attributes flow from that source, and you control precedence when a user is mastered by multiple sources.

Mappings define how profile attributes transform and flow between the Okta user profile and an app's profile (in either direction), using direct mappings or Okta Expression Language to convert or combine values.

flashcards.front: What do network zones and sign-on policies do?
flashcards.back: Network zones group IP ranges/locations (e.g. trusted office IPs) so policies can treat them differently. Sign-on policies use conditions like network zone, group, or device to decide whether to allow, deny, or require MFA for access.

flashcards.front: How does SSO differ from MFA, and which protocols enable SSO?
flashcards.back: SSO lets a user authenticate once and access many apps without re-logging in; MFA strengthens that authentication by requiring an additional factor. Okta delivers SSO to apps via SAML and OpenID Connect (OIDC).

questions.q: An organization sources user attributes from on-prem Active Directory and a cloud HR system and wants one consolidated profile per user that downstream apps can consume. Which Okta capability provides this single profile store?
choices: Universal Directory — one mastered profile aggregated from all sources
Okta Workflows — no-code automation for lifecycle events
API Access Management — OAuth scopes that secure custom APIs
Okta Verify — the mobile app for push and TOTP factors
questions.explanation: Universal Directory is Okta's single, flexible profile store. It aggregates and maps attributes from multiple sources (AD, HR systems, apps) into one master user profile that other applications read. Workflows automates lifecycle events, API Access Management secures custom APIs with OAuth, and Okta Verify is an MFA factor app — none of these is the consolidated profile store.

questions.q: A developer is building a new single-page web application that must sign users in and receive tokens to call protected back-end APIs. Which protocol should the Okta app integration use?
choices: LDAP, a directory query protocol for reading user records
RADIUS, an AAA protocol common to VPN and network access
OpenID Connect (OIDC) layered on OAuth 2.0
SAML 2.0 using the browser POST profile
questions.explanation: OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 and issues ID and access tokens, making it the right fit for modern SPAs and mobile apps that need to call APIs. SAML is XML-based browser SSO and does not issue OAuth API tokens. LDAP and RADIUS are not web SSO federation protocols.

questions.q: Security wants users prompted for a second factor only when they sign in from outside the corporate network, while in-office sign-ins skip MFA. What should the admin configure?
choices: A global rule that requires MFA for every sign-in regardless of location
A sign-on policy rule that requires MFA when the request is outside a trusted network zone
A password policy that increases minimum length for remote users
Self-service password reset enabled for all users
questions.explanation: Adaptive MFA is achieved with a sign-on policy rule whose condition references a network zone: when the request originates outside the trusted zone, the rule challenges for MFA; inside the zone, a separate rule can allow access without a factor. A blanket MFA rule ignores location, and password length or SSPR do not provide conditional MFA.

questions.q: In Okta, what does a Network Zone define?
choices: A group of applications that share one sign-on policy
A set of user lifecycle states such as staged and active
A collection of MFA factors a user has enrolled
A set of IP ranges or geolocations used as a condition in policies
questions.explanation: A network zone is a named set of IP address ranges (or dynamic geolocation/ASN criteria) that policies reference as a condition — for example to block, allow, or require MFA based on where a sign-in originates. It does not group apps, lifecycle states, or factors.

nodes.title: Identity lifecycle & SCIM provisioning: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Lifecycle management automates creating, updating, and deactivating user accounts in downstream apps as people join, move, and leave. SCIM is the open standard Okta uses to push these changes, a frequently-tested provisioning topic.

flashcards.front: What is SCIM and what does it automate?
flashcards.back: System for Cross-domain Identity Management is an open REST/JSON standard for exchanging identity data. Okta uses it to automatically provision, update, and deprovision user accounts and groups in downstream SaaS apps.
JIT creates or updates a user's account in a target app at the moment they first authenticate (e.g. via SAML/SCIM federation), rather than provisioning it ahead of time.

flashcards.front: How do group-based assignment and group rules work?
flashcards.back: Assigning an app to a group grants access to all its members automatically. Group rules use attribute conditions to dynamically add/remove users from groups, so access follows attribute changes without manual edits.

flashcards.front: How does Okta map the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle?
flashcards.back: Joiner: a new user is provisioned and assigned apps. Mover: profile/group changes update access automatically. Leaver: on offboarding the user is deactivated and accounts are deprovisioned in downstream apps to remove access.

questions.q: Okta should automatically create, update, and deactivate accounts in a downstream SaaS app as employees join, change roles, or leave. Which standard enables this automated provisioning?
choices: SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management)
SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)
questions.explanation: SCIM is the open standard Okta uses for lifecycle provisioning — pushing create, update, and deactivate operations to SCIM-enabled applications. SAML handles authentication/SSO, not account provisioning. SMTP is for email and SNMP for network device monitoring.

questions.q: Which Okta authentication factor offers phishing-resistant, passwordless sign-in using public-key cryptography that is cryptographically bound to the site's domain?
choices: SMS one-time passcode
Security question
FIDO2 / WebAuthn, such as a hardware security key
Email magic link
questions.explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn uses origin-bound public-key credentials, so a credential created for one domain cannot be replayed against a look-alike phishing site — making it phishing-resistant and passwordless. SMS codes, emailed links, and security questions can all be intercepted, phished, or guessed.

questions.q: How does Okta evaluate the rules within a sign-on policy?
choices: All rules are applied at once and the most restrictive result wins
Rules are evaluated top-down by priority, and the first matching rule is applied
Rules are evaluated in random order to balance load
Only the last rule in the list is ever applied
questions.explanation: Okta processes policy rules in priority order from top to bottom. The first rule whose conditions match the sign-in attempt is applied, and evaluation stops there. This is why rule order matters and why the catch-all default rule sits last.

questions.q: An admin wants users automatically added to the 'Sales' group whenever their department profile attribute equals 'Sales', with membership updating as the attribute changes. What should be used?
choices: A bookmark app pointing to the Sales portal
A network zone scoped to the Sales office IP ranges
A one-time manual static assignment of each user
A group rule that adds users based on the department attribute
questions.explanation: Group rules use a condition expression over profile attributes to dynamically add or remove members as those attributes change — ideal for keeping a 'Sales' group in sync with the department attribute. Static assignment is manual and does not auto-update, a bookmark app is just an SSO tile, and a network zone is an IP/location condition.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: To import users from on-prem Active Directory and delegate password validation to AD, which Okta component must be installed on a domain-joined Windows server?
choices: The Okta Active Directory (AD) Agent
The Okta LDAP Interface
Okta Access Gateway
The Okta RADIUS Server Agent
questions.explanation: The lightweight Okta AD Agent runs on a domain-joined server and handles AD user/group import plus delegated authentication. The LDAP Interface exposes Okta itself as an LDAP endpoint (the opposite direction), Access Gateway brokers SSO to on-prem header/Kerberos web apps, and the RADIUS Server Agent adds Okta MFA to RADIUS clients like VPNs.

questions.q: An admin needs to investigate why several users were denied access yesterday and review their MFA challenges and policy evaluations. Where should they look?
choices: The Universal Directory profile editor
The Workflows console execution history
The System Log
The Applications assignment tab
questions.explanation: The System Log is Okta's central audit trail of authentication, MFA, policy evaluation, provisioning, and admin events, with rich filtering for troubleshooting. The profile editor manages attributes, Workflows history only shows flow executions, and the assignment tab manages who has an app — none of these capture sign-in/MFA events.

questions.q: With delegated authentication to Active Directory enabled, where is a user's password verified when they sign in to Okta?
choices: Against the password hash stored in Okta's Universal Directory
Against Active Directory, via the Okta AD agent
Against the downstream SaaS application's local database
Against a one-time passcode generated by Okta Verify
questions.explanation: With delegated authentication, Okta does not store the password; it passes the entered credentials through the AD agent to Active Directory, which validates them. This keeps AD as the system of record for passwords. Okta only stores a password hash when delegated auth is off and passwords are sourced/synced into Okta.

questions.q: A legacy web app supports no federation protocol — it only has a standard username and password login form. How can Okta still provide single sign-on to it?
choices: Configure SAML 2.0 federation with the app
Enable SCIM provisioning to the app
Add the app as an OpenID Connect client
Use Secure Web Authentication (SWA), where Okta securely stores and replays the credentials
questions.explanation: Secure Web Authentication (SWA) lets Okta provide SSO to apps that lack any federation support by securely storing the user's credentials and auto-filling/submitting the login form via the browser plugin. SAML and OIDC both require the app to support those protocols, and SCIM handles provisioning, not sign-in.
